entries.title: Consumer advocacy groups oppose Illinois American Water $142.4M rate hike and potential major acquisition
entries.summary: <p>Consumer advocates want Illinois American Water to cut its proposed $142.4 million rate hike by 38%, saying the company is seeking exorbitant profits.</p><p>Those advocates are seeking a $54 million cut to the proposal, according to filings to the Illinois Commerce Commission from the Illinois Attorney General’s office and groups including the Citizens Utility Board. The Illinois Commerce Commission is set to rule on the company’s request later this year.</p><p>Illinois American’s proposal, filed earlier this year, was submitted after the Illinois Commerce Commission approved a separate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2024/12/07/utility-illinois-american-water-will-increase-water-rates-in-2025" >$110 million rate increase for the company for 2025</a>. Illinois American’s proposal could bump water bills by an average of $168 per year for residential water customers and $336 per year for wastewater customers, according to CUB estimates.</p><p>The groups argue that Illinois American’s request for an increased payout for its investors — 10.75%, the same figure the ICC reduced by nearly a full percentage point in its last rate case — is driving the rising costs, saying it’s overinflated by $30.8 million when IAW's parent company has seen <a class="Link" href="https://ir.amwater.com/news-and-events/financial-releases/financial-release-details/2026/AMERICAN-WATER-REPORTS-STRONG-2025-RESULTS-AFFIRMS-2026-EPS-GUIDANCE-AND-LONG-TERM-TARGETS/default.aspx" target="_blank" >more than $1 billion dollars in profit each of the last two years</a>. </p><p>Meanwhile, as of April, nearly 47,000 households are already behind on their bills to Illinois American Water, totaling more than $8 million, according to ICC data.</p><p>“The fact that [the current return on investment] is not enough for them already is troubling,” said Eric DuBellis, general counsel for CUB.</p><p>In a statement to the Sun-Times, the company attributed the request for a rate increase to the cost of "replacing aging pipes, upgrading treatment facilities, improving storage and pumping systems, and meeting evolving regulatory requirements."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2024/12/07/utility-illinois-american-water-will-increase-water-rates-in-2025" >Utility Illinois American Water will increase water rates in 2025</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/03/23/can-replacing-illinois-toxic-lead-pipes-create-more-jobs" >Can replacing Illinois’ toxic lead pipes lead to a workforce boom?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But in addition to $4.7 million in executive bonuses factored into the request, CUB said the company also is basing its revenue estimates on a sharp drop in water use, akin to the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, when people stopped leaving their homes.</p><p>“It’s an absurd thing to forecast — that was an unforeseeable circumstance in an otherwise normal year,” DuBellis said.</p><p>Illinois American serves 148 communities across the state, including some in suburban Chicago. It operates the water delivery systems in those communities, along with 18 water treatment plants and 17 wastewater treatment facilities around the state.</p><p>Even beyond the rate hike, IAW and Aqua Illinois, two of the largest water utility providers in the state, proposed an acquisition that would put the two under the same roof last October; the Illinois Commerce Commission still has yet to rule on it.</p><p>Over the last several years, the two companies have aggressively bought up depreciated municipal water and wastewater systems, which CUB says has added $411 million to Illinois water bills since 2013.</p><p>IAW has also purchased Prairie Path Water Company, which has about 35,000 customers in northern and central Illinois. If the proposed acquisition is approved, it would leave just about 800 private residential water customers outside IAW’s jurisdiction statewide — an effective monopoly for water utility and a complete monopoly for wastewater, according to CUB.</p><p>The “level of market consolidation raises obvious concerns,” representatives for CUB wrote in ICC filings.</p><p>“It would make one large private utility in the state,” Bryan McDaniel, CUB's director of governmental affairs. “They’re buying all these systems, there’ll be no competition, just one big monopoly.”</p><p>The consumer advocate also argues the consolidation of utilities has led to worse outcomes for customers.</p><p>Data from Aqua Illinois in ICC filings show a 77% increase in “unplanned disruptions” — such as main breaks — from 2022 to 2025, as well as a 39% increase in “unplanned advisories,” which include boil orders, between 2024 and 2025. CUB said data for advisories in 2022 and 2023 weren’t provided when requested by the Attorney General’s office as part of the case for the rate hike.</p><p>“Customers pay the full price of the system, plus they replace it all,” McDaniel said. “We think shareholders ought to pay for that.”</p><p>CUB has been pushing for legislative action to make the companies pay for the acquisitions, and State Sen. Laura Murphy had legislation up for consideration to force the utility companies’ shareholders to shoulder 80% of merger and acquisition costs. It had been inspired by stories she had heard from constituents in Des Plaines.</p><p>Between July 2024 and 2025, IAW customers in Des Plaines saw bills an average of 142% higher than those getting water from the municipal system, according to a study conducted by the city of Des Plaines.</p><p>The legislation was amended after push back, opting instead to give towns and cities a chance to buy back their systems every few years, but still didn’t pass by the end of the session. The problem persists, Murphy said, as she still constantly hears of complaints out of Des Plaines.</p><p>“I remember when it was rare when a utility went to the ICC [for a rate hike], people’s salaries can't keep up, ” Murphy said. “You have to learn how to manage the same way the government does. You don't have to have profits to increase upper management salaries.”</p><p>While that bill is stalled until the next time the legislature convenes, Murphy said her colleagues have been looking into reforming the current rate hike system and bolsering the ICC’s ability to regulate utilities for the fall session.</p><p>IAW’s request comes at the same time Peoples Gas’ put in for a $202 million rate hike and Nicor for a $220 million rate hike; both also will be up for a vote before the ICC later this year.</p><p>“Our system structure puts the ICC as that watchdog and they're going to have to step up like they never have before,” Murphy said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/05/06/illinois-attorney-general-kwame-raoul-rate-cut-request-peoples-gas-202m-hike-proposal" >Illinois attorney general pushes for rate cut as Peoples Gas seeks $202 million hike</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/05/18/nicors-gas-rate-hike" >Consumer advocates turn up heat against $220M Nicor rate hate</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Obama Presidential Center set to start welcoming up to 1 million visitors per year
entries.summary: <p></p><p>The Obama Presidential Center has begun welcoming some of the first visitors of up to a million per year that are estimated to visit the Jackson Park museum, community center and park area, which will hold a grand opening on Juneteenth.</p><p>Following a series of “soft opening” events over the past month, officials gave reporters an early look <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/06/02/museum-tower-obama-presidential-center-maligned-signature-building-worthy-consideration" >inside the eight-floor museum</a> Wednesday, where Obama Foundation CEO Valerie Jarrett isn’t softening any expectations.</p><p>“This is an economic engine, not just for the South Side of Chicago … most certainly here, but it's going to be an engine for the city and the region,” Jarrett said. “It's going to be a beacon of hope to the world at a time where I think we can all use a little hope.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> campus.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>It’s been a long time coming for the $850 million presidential center, a sprawling concept first announced more than a decade ago, centered around the museum that chronicles the rise of Barack Obama from Chicago’s community organizing circles to the White House along with South Side-born first lady Michelle Obama.</p><p>The surrounding campus includes a playground, green space, sledding hill, public art installations, public forum, Chicago Public Library branch and an athletic facility, among other attractions in the heart of historic Jackson Park.</p><p>“There was a little controversy about building these beautiful buildings in a park,” Jarrett said, paraphrasing years of federal reviews, lawsuits filed by parkland advocates and neighborhood activists demanding community benefits agreements.</p><p>“It's important for you to know that because we tore out Cornell Drive, which separated us from the Museum of Science and Industry, we have 3.7 additional acres of parkland that wasn’t here before,” Jarrett said, underscoring the breathtaking vistas of the park and city from the museum’s eighth floor. “That view really tells the story about Chicago.”</p><p>Longtime City Hall leader and incoming Obama Presidential Center executive vice president John Roberson touted 5,000 construction jobs created through the privately funded institution, the most expensive presidential center ever built, with a lengthy list of top donors including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Airbnb founder Brian Chesky.</p><p>“It's this level of investment that has been lacking on the South and West sides for way too long. And the president and Mrs. Obama understood what bringing that level of investment would mean to our city,” Roberson said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div entries.title: Obama Presidential Center delivers a lesson in democracy — and what it means to be a country in progress
entries.summary: <p>The Obama Presidential Center is full of intriguing juxtapositions, starting with its address.</p><p>The site in tribute to the country’s first Black president sits on parkland named after a former slave owning president.</p><p>Democracy is the throughline in museum exhibitions and programming, even as the nonpartisan organization behind the complex, the Obama Foundation, remains mum about the current White House administration and distances itself from weighing in on electoral politics.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" And while a museum touting democracy may feel insufficient for young people piloting through perilous times, Obama Foundation CEO Valerie Jarrett said<b> </b>Wednesday in a press preview that a sense of discovery awaits them.</p><p>“They'll discover that ordinary people have the capability to do extraordinary things if they put their mind to it, through the stories that we tell of the history of our country, which has been really challenging at times,” said Jarrett sitting in kitchen classroom near the Eleanor Roosevelt fruit and vegetable garden and a Rashid Johnson mosaic in the campus.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The garden is one of several features on a site anchored by community play spaces, a hoops center and a museum that covers social movements.</p><p>“We've always had a very strong North Star in terms of our mission, which is to inspire, empower, and connect people to change their world,” said Louise Bernard, museum director. “One of the takeaways we often reference is this idea of what it means to bring change home. So the center is really a hub that draws people in and then sends them out.”</p><p>Instead of Barack Obama’s journey to Chicago or Michelle Obama’s glamorous dresses — upper museum floors dive into those narratives — the story begins with America as a work in progress. Contradictions of the Founding Fathers and democracy as an ambitious radical experiment first greet visitors. Questions prompt guests to consider freedom, rights and class. Words from abolitionist/suffragist Frances Ellen Watkins Harper, the Cherokee Nation and labor leader Dolores Huerta underscore the unfilled promises of the nation.</p><div class="Enhancement" Those areas are gun control after the Sandy Hook massacre, comprehensive immigration reform and removing mandatory minimum sentences for nonviolent drug offenders.</p><p>Over the last decade, the Obamas articulated a steadfast urban vision for the South Side. The 19-acre campus is free to the public. It features gardens and winding walking paths, grills and benches designed by students at Simeon Career Academy. Community members suggested a new Chicago Public Library branch and now there’s one. The former first lady grew up in nearby South Shore and lamented the lack of sledding; the playground area at OPC offers a sledding hill. She also pointed out the lack of public art, so OPC commissioned 28 pieces by some of the biggest contemporary art names: Richard Hunt, Carrie Mae Weems, Alison Saar and Julie Mehretu.</p><p>“We think about that relationship between art and health and wellness, the visceral impact that art can have on the body. photographic collage with blue tonal overlays.</p><p>“Art is the creative expression of our imaginations and our feelings. It is the expressive part of culture, the expressive part of ideas, and it's not just about now, but it's about always,” Weems said. The piece’s first image is from the 54th regiment that fought in the Civil War. The end is a group of young people dancing during the Civil Rights Movement.</p><p>“In between is a suite of ideas,” Weems said. “For me the piece is joyous and spontaneous and warm and inviting and welcoming and celebratory — and that’s ultimately what democracy is. entries.summary: <h2>Moon Alert</h2> <p>After 9 a.m., there are no restrictions to spending or making important decisions. The moon moves to Aquarius.</p><h2>Aries (March 21-April 19)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-7b0000" name="html-embed-module-7b0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>A <b>positive</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> This is an interesting day because you have strong feelings about something (which you will no doubt share with a friend or a group) — feelings that might relate to doing something spontaneously to express your desire for freedom or to discover something new and exciting. "Who's with me?"</p><h2>Taurus (April 20-May 20)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> A surprise interaction with the police, a parent or a boss — or anyone in authority — might catch you off guard today. Tread carefully because feelings are strong today and some people will be adamant about what they want — and they want it yesterday. Softly, softly.</p><h2>Gemini (May 21-June 20)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-7b0000" name="html-embed-module-7b0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>A <b>positive</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> Steer clear of controversial subjects today because people are obsessed with their opinions, which means you might get caught in a power struggle with someone, or they might be determined to make you agree with them. Yikes! Run away!</p><h2>Cancer (June 21-July 22)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> Double-check banking details because something unexpected could impact your wealth, your assets or something to do with shared property or inheritances. Naturally, you care about your assets and will be upset if something goes wrong. Stay calm.</p><h2>Leo (July 23-Aug. 22)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-7b0000" name="html-embed-module-7b0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>A <b>positive</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> Today you might attract someone who has strong opinions. This person could be a character or someone you suddenly met. Don't let anyone bulldoze you with their ideas. After all, you have ideas of your own, right?</p><h2>Virgo (Aug. 23-Sept. 22)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> Be careful you don't come on too strong with work colleagues today in your enthusiasm to make improvements or get rid of what is no longer working. Your impulse to clean things might be misunderstood. People can feel threatened by change — even change for the better.</p><h2>Libra (Sept. 23-Oct. 22)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-7b0000" name="html-embed-module-7b0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>A <b>positive</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> A romantic interest might suddenly develop today — something out of the blue. Furthermore, it's passionate and irresistible. Others might have a similar surprise related to sports or something to do with your kids or the arts. Take a breath and get grounded. Do you need some perspective?</p><h2>Scorpio (Oct. 23-Nov. 21)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> Family discussions are intense today because someone really wants their way. It could relate to a sudden decision about inheritances, shared property, taxes or debt. Whatever the issue, there are strong feelings around it. Why not wait until things settle down before committing?</p><h2>Sagittarius (Nov. 22-Dec. 21)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-7b0000" name="html-embed-module-7b0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>A <b>positive</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> You might get on your high horse today because you are convinced about something and have very strong feelings about it. It could be triggered by a partner or close friend doing something that catches you off guard. Don't overreact. entries.title: Man charged in fatal DUI crash that killed tollway worker fixing potholes on I-294
entries.summary: <p>A Berwyn man has been charged in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/31/tollway-worker-killed-two-hurt-i-294" >a crash this past weekend</a> that killed one tollway worker and hospitalized two others, according to the Illinois State Police.</p><p>Paul Ong, 37, faces a felony count of aggravated driving under the influence involving death, police said.</p><p>The three tollway workers had been filling potholes in the southbound lanes of I-294 north of Devon Avenue at 4:26 a.m. Saturday when one of them was struck by a vehicle, police said. All three were taken to a nearby hospital. The worker who was struck died. The others suffered “non-life threatening injuries,” police said.</p><p>The worker who died was identified as Calvin L. Holley, 52, of the Dunning neighborhood, according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p>

entries.title: Spencer Leak helped countless people after relatives' deaths, now many are trying to comfort his family
entries.summary: <p>Over a span of decades, Spencer Leak Jr. comforted thousands of grieving families in their most trying moments as he helped run Leak & Sons Funeral Homes — an institution on the South Side.</p><p>Since his unexpected death Sunday, his family has heard from many of them. There's been an avalanche of calls, texts, social media messages, hot meals and sweet treats sent by those whose lives he touched, sharing their gratitude and their sorrow.</p><p>"We're so appreciative, especially considering the family's role has been to comfort so many other families for so many years, the support we're receiving, it's nourishing to our souls," said Mr. Leak's wife, Donna Leak. "And it's helping us to stay focused and grounded."</p><p>Mr. Leak, 56, hadn't been feeling well in recent days, according to his wife, who said he'd felt ill and went to an urgent-care center a few days before his death. He was recovering at home from what was chalked up as a gastrointestinal virus.</p><p>But he was found unresponsive at his home in Flossmoor on Sunday morning, and paramedics taking him to a hospital in Olympia Fields couldn't revive him, his wife said.</p><p>"He died peacefully in his sleep," she said, adding that the family is waiting for answers on the cause of death.</p><p>"It's devastating," she said. "But we are a strong family, a close family, and we're holding ourselves together, staying prayed up and staying thankful to God for the time we had."</p><p>Nykea Pippion was among the thousands who have offered condolences on Facebook. Pippion said Mr. Leak was there for her after her 23-year-old son Xavier Joy was fatally shot by someone trying to steal his cell phone in 2017 on the South Side. He attended Whitney Young High School and Morehouse College and was back in Chicago doing volunteer work when he was killed. His father, Ra Joy, was Chris Kennedy's gubernatorial running mate in 2018.</p><p>"I can't even put into words," Pippion said. "He genuinely cared for my son like it was his son, and I was his sister. There were a lot of media people and elected officials at the service, and Spencer made sure I had water, that I could walk to the restroom or go get some air and was just present over and above anything I would have expected."</p><p>Mr. Leak coordinated a New Orleans style jazz funeral for Joy, with a brass band and a parade leading down the street from the University of Chicago's Rockefeller Chapel, where the services were held.</p><p>"He personally was there and made sure everything went smoothly even though there were more than 2,000 people there — he wanted my son's sendoff to be meticulously executed, and it was," Pippion said. "And he followed up with me randomly after that with text messages, just checking in on me to see if I was doing all right."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Leak helped run the family business for more than 45 years.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Mr. Leak started working at the funeral home when he was just 12 years old. His grandfather A.R. Leak had started the business in 1933, and Mr. Leak learned under his father, Spencer Leak Sr.</p><p>"Being a funeral director is a calling, and that's how he felt about it, and not everyone can do it," Donna Leak said. "Every day of your life, you're comforting people who are having the worst day of their life, and somehow God gives you the passion to do it and not have it deplete you." </p><p>In recent years, Mr. Leak took over handling calls with people who couldn't afford a funeral for a loved one but knew they could come to the Leak family to work something out.</p><p>"Ever since our grandfather started the business in 1933, his whole motto was just to make sure that, if an African American family didn't have the means to bury their loved ones, they could come to us and get a respectable burial," said Stacy Leak, Mr. Leak's brother.</p><p>Despite the grief and sadness all around, or perhaps because of it, Mr. Leak filled his life with joy. He occasionally held birthday parties for himself at the downtown Hyatt Regency. Last year, when he turned 55, more than 4,000 people came. Guests were asked to donate a winter coat for someone less fortunate.</p><p>He also held an annual barbecue at his house in Flossmoor and loved attending the Chosen Few house music festival.</p><p>"When you see so much hurt and pain and death, you want to celebrate life," his brother said.</p><p>Mr. Leak also loved collecting classic cars. An old burgundy Cadillac was one of his favorites.</p><p>With three Leak family funeral homes — at 7838 S. Cottage Grove Ave., as well as in Matteson and Country Club Hills — Mr. Leak routinely worked seven-day weeks, took calls at all hours, but made time to attend his daughter's dance recitals and son's football games, often in the black suit and gold tie he'd worn to work.</p><p>He loved beach vacations in the Bahamas and spoiling his dog Lambo. When Lambo was attacked by a coyote last year, Mr. Leak posted videos on Facebook about the misadventure, expressing how happy he was that she survived and how thankful he was for his brother's help in searching for her at night near his home.</p><p>"He was just so caring and kind," Stacy Leak said.</p><p>Funeral services for Mr. Leak were still being arranged.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/05/31/spencer-leak-jr-sons-funeral-homes-dies" >Spencer Leak Jr. of Leak and Sons Funeral Homes, who handled funerals of Rev. entries.title: Chicago youth call for more attention to missing Black girls, women
entries.summary: <p>Demonstrators dedicated Wednesday’s annual “We Walk for Her” march in Bronzeville to call for a city or statewide office focused solely on investigating missing and murdered Black girls and women.</p><p>Black women and girls account for around 30% of Cook County’s missing persons despite making up about 12% of the county’s population, according to the Cook County sheriff’s office and census estimates.</p><p>“When I see one of these missing persons flyers on these poles, I don’t just see a photo,” said Crystal Young, a youth intern with Kenwood-Oakland Community Organization. “I see a girl who looked like me, someone who had big dreams and someone whose family is now in a nightmare. I’m tired of us being treated like we’re invisible.”</p><p>“We’re here to say we are not just data points or percentages on a report,” Young added. “We are daughters, sisters and friends. We are human beings who deserve to grow up, be safe, and be protected. We deserve to walk through our own neighborhoods without wondering if we’ll make it home.”</p><p>Raising awareness for missing and murdered Black women and girls is crucial because their cases are treated by police and media with less importance than those of white persons, organizers said. And Black residents have historically gone missing at disproportionate rates.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Craig Counsell not sitting Dansby Swanson just yet, but it’s under consideration as Cubs keep losing
entries.summary: <p>Frustrated fans watching <b>Dansby Swanson</b>’s batting average plummet well below .200 are wondering when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> is going to sit his starting shortstop.</p><p>It didn’t happen Wednesday, with Swanson actually bumped up in the order to the No. 6 spot. His second-inning double in a 5-4 loss to the Athletics was just his fifth hit in his last 12 games.</p><p>But such a move is hardly off the table should Swanson’s slump continue.</p><p>“You certainly consider all those things,” Counsell said, “and you think about them [and whether it’s] the right time and if it’s necessary. All those things, you think about.”</p><p>It’s far from the strongest language the Cubs’ skipper could have used. But he’s already employed the tactic with a struggling veteran, sitting left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> in back-to-back games last month.</p><p>Happ was in a brutal stretch at the time, hitting .148 over 17 games, before getting a couple games in a row off. Since, he’s been one of the team’s better hitters, batting .316 with eight extra-base hits in nine games.</p><p>The whole season has seemed a brutal stretch for Swanson, and his .181 batting average was the third lowest among baseball’s qualified hitters coming into Wednesday.</p><p>But while <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/01/cubs-dansby-swanson-slump-stats-defense-craig-counsell-lineup" >Swanson’s ugly numbers</a> have made him a lightning rod for complaints, he’s far from the only thing wrong with the Cubs’ offense, which has looked broken for the last few weeks.</p><p>There’s plenty of blame to go around after the Cubs dropped the first two games of their series with the A’s. They’re 5-18 in their last 23 contests.</p><p>“We’re not winning a lot of baseball games right now,” Counsell said after Wednesday’s extra-inning loss. “We’re not playing well enough to win a lot of baseball games. You have to earn it, and we’re not earning it. It’s not some string of massive bad luck. We’re not earning wins, flat out.</p><p>“Losing stinks, so that gets to you. There’s no sugarcoating that.”</p><p>Counsell did make the decision to pinch hit for Swanson late Tuesday, sending <b>Moises Ballesteros</b> to the plate, citing Ballesteros’ ability to hit the ball out of the ballpark on a night where runs were at a premium.</p><p>Showing how rough things have been team-wide, Ballesteros didn’t seem like that much better of an option. He has struggled mightily, too, in the middle of a 6-for-69 stretch.</p><p>“This isn’t going to continue for Dansby. He’s going to be better,” Counsell said. “We’re just at a moment in time right now. I don’t think [pinch hitting for him is] going to happen very often. He’s going to be better.”</p><p><b>Time on their side?</b></p><p>The Cubs’ recent stretch of ugly results has fans worried, especially considering the team’s championship-level expectations.</p><p>“The expectations are super high. And this doesn’t change it,” starting pitcher <b>Colin Rea</b> said Wednesday. “Once we break out of this stretch, it’s going to be fun. It’s going to be a lot of fun to be a part of, and we’re going to do some cool things.”</p><p>That might be a hard sell for fans who have sat through the last few weeks. The Cubs have gone eight consecutive series without a series win.</p><p>But there are 100 games left on the schedule.</p><p>“Anybody would be lying to you if they were saying they weren’t frustrated right now,” relief pitcher <b>Phil Maton</b> told the Sun-Times. “Hopefully, this is just a blip on the radar and we look back in a month and say, ‘Man, I can’t believe we were going through it like that.’”</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-c90005" name="list-c90005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, titleUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, inverseColors=false, items=[{description=[{items=[Bregman, who got a $175 million free-agent contract last winter, brought a reputation as a strong clubhouse presence. entries.title: Contralora estatal Susana Mendoza se postula para alcaldesa y critica a Johnson y al secretrio Giannoulias
entries.summary: <p>Argumentando que Chicago necesita "liderazgo competente" —no un alcalde que "protege a los criminales" y que responde a los intereses del Sindicato de Maestros de Chicago— la Contralora de Illinois Susana Mendoza se unió oficialmente el miércoles a la abarrotada contienda por la alcaldía de Chicago.</p><p>Mendoza terminó en quinto lugar en la <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/4/3/18349334/lightfoot-meets-with-emanuel-to-begin-transition-after-landslide-win" target="_blank" >contienda por la alcaldía de 2019</a> ganada por Lori Lightfoot y que estuvo dominada por el escándalo de corrupción que culminó en la condena del ex concejal del 14.° distrito Edward Burke.</p><p>Ganó sólo siete de los 50 distritos en 2019, casi todos de mayoría hispana/latina, y obtuvo poco más del 9% de los votos. Su larga alianza con Burke y el ahora condenado Presidente de la Cámara de Representantes de Illinois, Michael Madigan, demócrata por Chicago, le causó un gran daño.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-140000" name="module-140000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Pero Mendoza le dijo al Chicago Sun-Times que es una candidata mucho más experimentada que aquella que terminó detrás de Lightfoot, la Presidenta de la Junta del Condado de Cook, Toni Preckwinkle, el exjefe de gabinete de la Casa Blanca, Bill Daley, y el empresario Willie Wilson.</p><p>Mendoza argumentó que su "tríada de experiencia" como legisladora estatal, secretaria de la Municipalidad y contralora estatal demuestra que es la "experta en transformación" que Chicago necesita para resolver sus problemas financieros y de seguridad pública, así como su "crisis de confianza" bajo la gestión actual de Brandon Johnson.</p><p>“Necesitamos un alcalde que no proteja a los criminales, sino que los haga responsables y cambie el rumbo moral de esta ciudad para poner a las víctimas por delante de los infractores. Ese es un punto clave de fracaso para esta administración”, dijo Mendoza, de 54 años.</p><p>“La más obvia que todos sienten… es la crisis financiera en la que estamos. Y no hay nadie mejor ubicado para arreglar las finanzas de la ciudad que alguien que arregló las del estado cuando muchas personas pensaban que era una tarea imposible. Ese es mi fuerte”, dijo Mendoza.</p><p>El fondo de campaña de Mendoza, de $1.6 millones, palidece en comparación con el de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/04/16/brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-susana-mendoza-potential-mayoral-bids-campaign-fundraising" target="_blank" >$18.3 millones</a> que ya ha acumulado el Secretario de Estado de Illinois, Alexi Giannoulias, un potencial candidato a la alcaldía.</p><p>Pero Mendoza, quien <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/07/17/susana-mendoza-no-buscara-la-reeleccion-y-considera-postularse-para-alcaldesa" target="_blank" >optó por no postularse nuevamente</a> para contralora este año,dijo que no se siente intimidada por la capacidad de recaudación de fondos de Giannoulias o las grandes contribuciones que ha recibido de sindicatos de la construcción. Añadió que tampoco se dejará presionar para salir de la carrera por un candidato que parece estar jugando a lo seguro y permanecer al margen.</p><p>“¿No está postulándose para secretario de estado? No ha declarado [que sea para alcalde]. Yo estoy postulándome para alcaldesa de Chicago, y no me importa quién se meta en esta carrera”, aseguró.</p><p>“Nadie puede igualar mi experiencia financiera. Nadie puede igualar mi conocimiento para hacer las cosas en Springfield... No tengo que pedirle permiso a nadie para expresar mis ideas. Voy a manejar esta ciudad mejor que cualquier otro gerente ejecutivo lo ha hecho en el pasado. Y eso lo puedes llevar al banco. Sólo que no al Broadway Bank”, el banco ahora cerrado que una vez fue propiedad de la familia Giannoulias y que una vez lo empleó, comentó.</p><p>Johnson aún no ha declarado su intención de buscar un segundo mandato. Su índice de aprobación sigue en los bajos 30, y sólo tiene $813,125 en efectivo de campaña disponibles.</p><p>Su capacidad para recaudar fondos probablemente se verá obstaculizada por la reciente decisión de las bases del Sindicato de Maestros de Chicago (CTU) de rechazar el aumento de cuotas de membresía de $8.5 millones promovido por la Presidenta del CTU, Stacy Davis Gates.</p><p>Pero el cuestionado alcalde aún tiene toda la franja de la izquierda para sí mismo, y es el único candidato afroamericano destacado considerando unirse a la contienda.</p><p>Mendoza y Giannoulias están compitiendo por los votantes en la misma franja moderada. Eso explica por qué Mendoza parecía estar atacando a Giannoulias tanto como a Johnson.</p><p>“No nací con una cuchara de plata en la boca. Nací más bien [con] una cuchara de plástico, y la gente se identifica con eso. Saben quién es legítimo. Saben quién puede relacionarse con ellos, quién es auténtico”, aseguró. “Hay una gran diferencia entre eso y alguien que sostiene la mano del portero mientras él presiona el botón para llevarlo a su rascacielos”.</p><p>Giannoulias no pudo ser contactado para hacer comentarios.</p><p>Johnson intentó una vez más mantenerse por encima de la contienda política.</p><p>"Ningún alcalde en la historia moderna puede decir que supervisó la Ciudad de Chicago en el auge del desarrollo y actividad económicos, donde más personas están visitando nuestra ciudad que en cualquier otro momento en la historia de Chicago. Y acabamos de registrar el nivel más bajo de homicidios en 60 años”, dijo el alcalde. “Ese es el trabajo que estoy haciendo, y voy a continuar concentrado en eso".</p><p>El veterano operador político Víctor Reyes dijo que la enérgica entrada de Mendoza en la carrera podría intensificar la presión sobre Giannoulias para que abandone la zona de seguridad y se meta en la contienda.</p><p>“Van a tener que proteger ese punto débil. No se puede tratar de sólo estar contra Johnson. Tarde o temprano van a tener que bajar los números de Susana”, dijo Reyes. “Cada día que se retrasen es una ventaja para Johnson”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Will Chicago happily eat dolmades and drink roditis in Trump Tower?
entries.summary: <p>In southern Greece, at the foot of Mount Artemisio, is a tiny village called Nestani. About 500 people live there, some still herding goats, as did their fathers and grandfathers before. Above the town, built into the imposing Rock of Goulas, is a monastery, founded in the 13th century. And on the gate of that monastery is an inscription, honoring the women of "Sikago" for their generosity sending money back for renovations.</p><p>Local lore insists that more people born in Nestani live in Chicago than live in the village itself. Many came here over the past century and made a good living. </p><p>One of them is Petros Kogiones, whose Dianna's Opaa was a beloved fixture on Halsted Street from the mid-1970s to the mid-1990s.</p><p>"From every other house somebody came to America, came to Chicago," Kogiones, 89, remembered when I phoned to chat. "Some had coffee shops or candy shops."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-230000" name="module-230000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Why did Greeks go into food service?</p><p>"It was the natural thing to do," said Kogiones. "For Greeks, it was the easiest thing. With a lack of language, what else could they do? Wash the dishes. Cooking, like me."</p><p>Dianna's closed 30 years ago. But we are still a city blessed with excellent Greek restaurants. My favorite, Psistaria Greek Taverna on Touhy, is a boisterous room. Lively service. And great food. The chicken spanaki. The center cut pork chops. The green beans.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7d0000" name="image-7d0000"></a> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chicago already has lots of excellent Greek restaurants, such as the super wonderful Psistaria Greek Taverna in Lincolnwood. It’s about to get another one. In Trump Tower.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Neil Steinberg</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Chicago's Greektown was decimated by the twin blows of UIC and expressway expansion. But there are still plenty of Greek eateries on the shred that remained: Greek Islands and Athena and Artopolis Bakery, where I would reverently visit to stock up on <i>melomakarona,</i> those luscious honey cookies, before diabetes made the practice unwise.</p><p>And those are just the old school places. There are many newer Greek restaurants like Lyra in Fulton Market and Elia in Bucktown. </p><p>With more coming.<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/06/01/trump-international-hotel-tower-first-retail-tenant-prasino-17-years" target="_blank" > In Tuesday’s paper,</a> we learned that a La Grange restaurant, Prasino, is opening in the base of Trump Tower.</p><p>Normally, I'd welcome any addition to the Greek restaurant pantheon, particularly one as centrally located as Wabash just north of the river.</p><p>But these are not normal times. My immediate reaction to the news was, "Did you you read the room?" Restaurants are more than food and service and a nice setting. Karma is involved. They tore down the Brown's Fried Chicken in Palatine where seven employees were massacred in 1993 because nobody wanted to eat there after that. </p><p>As to whether Trump Tower deserves the same level of ignominy, well, I guess that depends on how dearly you cherish American values and traditions. I happen to cherish them a lot. But I also know that I'm not the only person in the world.</p><p>"We view this as a hospitality investment, not a political statement," Prasino owner Ted Maglaris told the paper.</p><p>Give the man credit. He bit at a baited hook that has dangled for 17 years in front of every restaurant group in Chicago: Lettuce Entertain You and Boka and Gibsons. None of them hazarded a nibble. It takes a certain kind of courage to make your hospitality investment there, to plant that hook in your cheek, eyes wide open.</p><p>"It's not about blue, not about red," the property leasing agent, Jason Pruger, added. "The most American thing is green... It's about making money."</p><p>He's got that right. That certainly is the philosophy of our elected officials turning the United States government into a personal piggy bank. They are making money big time.</p><p>But going to restaurants for most of us is not about making money, but spending it. And knowing that part of the price of my avgolemono soup is going to pay rent to the Trump Organization, well... bad enough I have to pay taxes that pay the salaries of Stephen Miller and JD Vance. Yes, Kogiones would praise Nixon in the little speeches he gave every night at 9 p.m. at Dianna's. But this is different.</p><p>Are the people lining up to take selfies flipping the bird at Trump Tower going to upload their shots onto social media then hurry into Prasino for moussaka? Maybe. Maybe the crowd from Orland Park and Burr Ridge will slap on their red MAGA hats and go show support for the president by ordering the imported sea bream. They exist, and I'm sure to hear from them. "Steengold — thank you for alerting me to the pending arrival of Prasino — I will be going there with my Atomwaffen Division cell to celebrate next April 20!"</p><p>I hate to rain on anybody's dream. Prasino is opening in early 2027. If there are free and fair elections in November 2028, I'll slide by the new restaurant for a celebratory meal. Underline that "if."</p>

entries.title: Ex-Bear Kyle Long to co-host "The NFL Today" on CBS
entries.summary: <p>Kyle Long grew up around NFL morning shows.</p><p>Now he’s hosting one on CBS.</p><p>The former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> offensive lineman was named one of the two new hosts of “The NFL Today” on Thursday, joining the newly retired Russell Wilson on the hourlong show that precedes CBS’ noon game. The addition of Long, whose father Howie is a staple on the Fox pregame show, was announced on “CBS Mornings.”</p><p>“It’s been my dream to work in this industry since visiting my dad in studio in 1994,” Long said in a statement. “From the moment I realized I wouldn’t play in the league forever, I’ve had my compass set for this job.”</p><p>Howie Long has hosted "Fox NFL Sunday" since its inception in 1994.</p><p>Long, who has worked across CBS Sports platforms since 2020, made occasional appearances on “The NFL Today” last year. Once former quarterback Matt Ryan was named the Falcons’ president of football, Long and quarterback Kirk Cousins worked playoff games in his place. Long also worked a Week 18 game in the booth.</p><p>A first-round pick of the Bears in 2013, Long made the Pro Bowl in each of his first three seasons, playing both guard and tackle. He spent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2020/6/15/21291766/fired-by-bears-former-offensive-lineman-kyle-long-considers-return-to-nfl" target="_blank" >seven years with the Bears</a> and played briefly with the Chiefs before retiring.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: At Simeon, a basketball powerhouse, drama students shine in school's first play in decades
entries.summary: <p>When Deonte Haywood arrived at Simeon Career Academy in the fall, the 14-year-old felt “shy about his height.” And he worried about finding his place among the many towering students who came to the basketball powerhouse with dreams of becoming the next Derrick Rose.</p><p>But Deonte found his crowd when a school counselor just happened to enroll him in a drama class. That class was tasked with putting on Simeon’s first full-length play in perhaps decades.</p><p>Despite his small stature, Deonte filled the stage as a Southern preacher in a fitted blue suit. He saw it as much more than a chance to be in the spotlight in a play by the famed August Wilson.</p><p>“It really gave me a chance to express myself,” he said. “I became friends with everybody and our bond grew stronger.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-930000" schools, the annual play is a staple and the experience is profound. For some students, it sparks dreams of being a professional thespian. For others, like Deonte, it is a safe place where students learn to work together and get to be part of something bigger than themselves.</p><p>Most Chicago public high schools have some type of arts performance for families to attend. But only 37 of the district’s 115 high schools reported offering a theatrical production last year, according to an <a class="Link" href="https://www.ingenuity-inc.org/data-research/state-of-the-arts-reports/2024-25/" target="_blank" ><u>annual survey done by Ingenuity Chicago</u></a>, an organization that advocates for equity in arts education across Chicago Public Schools.</p><p>Principal Tamarah Ellis cannot remember a play for as long as she’s been at Simeon. That includes when she went to Simeon as a student in the 1980s and taught there in the early 2000s. But when she took the helm last year, and the drama teacher asked her about putting on a play, she quickly decided she wanted to make it happen.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div give the kids something to celebrate. We have a lot of students that watch movies and they dream of having that opportunity. So, what better place to start rather than high school?”</p><p>Ellis doesn’t know why Simeon went without a play for so many years. The school is a career and technical academy known for its sports, especially basketball. It is likely that past principals focused on spending their limited discretionary funds on those programs.</p><p>Drama teacher David Hossler said it wasn’t until last year that he saw “a way forward to do a project like this.” At the time, he’d been teaching at Simeon for three years and it was his first teaching job.</p><p>Then, two things happened. He heard the Educational Theatre Foundation, which works to expand access to theater in schools, was offering $10,000 grants. And he got Ellis’ support to offer an upper-level drama class capable of putting on a play.</p><p>The school won the grant, and they used it to hire a director and buy materials so Simeon’s carpentry program could build the set. For Barfield, it was “A Raisin in the Sun,” Lorraine Hansberry’s acclaimed story about a Black family from Chicago’s South Side, at Corliss High School.</p><p>“Sadly, the arts are being taken out of a lot of schools,” she said. “But the arts are definitely important for the kids to find that creativity, give them a chance to express themselves and just overall brighten their horizons.”</p>

entries.title: FBI's high-tech hunt led to alleged bank robbery 'mastermind' killed in shootout on Chicago's West Side
entries.summary: <p>The alleged leader of a bank robbery crew killed in a shootout on the West Side last week was tracked down in a weekslong manhunt powered by surveillance cameras, tracking devices and cellphone monitoring.</p><p>Abdulhafedh Abdulhafedh, 25, was behind the wheel of a black Cadillac Escalade on May 28 when FBI agents boxed in the SUV on West Lexington Street, according to court records and officials.</p><p>What happened next was captured in part on a resident's cellphone video. Authorities say Abdulhafedh fired at agents through the roof of the Escalade. Agents returned fire, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/29/witness-hears-30-rifle-rounds-when-fbi-agents-in-riot-gear-gun-down-convicted-bank-robber-on-west-side" target="_blank" >killing him</a>.</p><p>The shootout capped an elaborate game of cat-and-mouse that unfolded after a series of armed bank robberies investigators linked to a crew that called itself the "100K Gang."</p><p>Federal authorities say Abdulhafedh was the "mastermind" the group, which is accused of stealing more than $201,000 during an armed robbery of a BMO Harris branch in St. Charles on April 21. An FBI affidavit alleges Abdulhafedh was also tied to five other BMO bank robberies across the Chicago area.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Abdulhafedh relied on a sophisticated web of technology — the same type of electronic sleuthing federal authorities used to track members of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/1/17/24040490/jury-verdict-fbg-duck-murder-gold-coast" target="_blank" >South Side gang</a> later convicted in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/1/28/22907047/fbg-duck-murder-case-gold-coast-o-block-street-gang" target="_blank" >2020 slaying of Chicago rapper FBG Duck</a>.</p><p>The trail began almost immediately after the St. Charles robbery.</p><p>Three masked robbers fled the bank in a Ford Fusion carrying cash stuffed into black plastic bags. Hidden among the money was an electronic tracking device, allowing St. Charles police to follow the getaway car in real time.</p><p>But the robbers appeared ready for that possibility.</p><p>The Ford was found abandoned and the tracking device had been tossed into the Fox River.</p><p>Even so, investigators caught a break.</p><p>A license plate reader mounted on a bridge over the Fox River captured an image of a Volkswagen SUV crossing moments later. The photo appeared to show someone extending an arm out the window — seemingly discarding the tracking device into the water below.</p><p>The Volkswagen's license plate led investigators to a residence on Chicago's West Side, according to court records.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-590000" name="image-590000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/30810ec/2147483647/strip/true/crop/916x514+0+138/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0b%2Fec%2Faa99af6245d58b9b0f07ea6af761%2Fscreenshot-2026-06-03-at-3-36-17-pm.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/330e6a1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/916x514+0+138/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0b%2Fec%2Faa99af6245d58b9b0f07ea6af761%2Fscreenshot-2026-06-03-at-3-36-17-pm.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/06bf480/2147483647/strip/true/crop/916x514+0+138/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0b%2Fec%2Faa99af6245d58b9b0f07ea6af761%2Fscreenshot-2026-06-03-at-3-36-17-pm.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The Volkswagen SUV photographed on a bridge over the Fox River in St. Charles. During the stop, agents found $32,000 in cash inside a backpack.</p><p>Court records don’t indicate whether anyone was arrested during the stop or whether authorities seized the money.</p><p>The investigation intensified weeks later when a Drug Enforcement Administration informant identified one of the robbery crew's alleged members as 18-year-old Dayvon Walton, according to the affidavit.</p><p>The informant told investigators the group was planning another bank robbery.</p><p>On May 19, the informant met Walton for breakfast to discuss plans for the next heist, authorities said.</p><p>The FBI secretly installed tracking devices in rental vehicles obtained through the informant for the planned robbery. But the crew never carried it out.</p><p>Federal agents then secured a court order allowing them to monitor the phones of Walton and Abdulhafedh.</p><p>At the time, Abdulhafedh had been out of prison for a few months after serving a four-year sentence for a 2021 attempted robbery of a BMO bank branch in New Lenox in Will County. He had been released on parole in January.</p><p>The electronic surveillance soon paid off.</p><p>On May 28, agents spotted Abdulhafedh leaving a house and getting into the Escalade. Investigators believed Walton was also inside.</p><p>Armed with a parole warrant, agents moved in.</p><p>According to the FBI, Abdulhafedh refused orders to exit the SUV after agents stopped it.</p><p>Authorities deployed smoke bombs into the vehicle.</p><p>Moments later, gunfire erupted.</p><p>Officials say <a class="Link" entries.title: White Sox rookie Jacob Gonzalez learning on the job in place of Munetaka Murakami
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> first baseman Jacob Gonzalez had a rough start to his first major-league road series. He struck out in his first six at-bats this week at Target Field, and the skid left him with an unfamiliar feeling.</p><p>“I don’t consider myself a person that strikes out a lot,” Gonzalez said Wednesday. “And then I struck out six times in a row — for the first time in my life, probably.</p><p>“I knew that it wasn’t gonna keep happening. I consider myself better than that. So I was just sticking to what I was doing, and I knew that it wouldn’t happen a seventh time.”</p><p>It didn’t. In his third at-bat Tuesday against the Twins, the left-handed-hitting Gonzalez grounded a single to right field. In his fourth at-bat, he walked, against a left-hander, no less.</p><p>Now he was on to something.</p><p>In his first at-bat Wednesday, Gonzalez lined a single the other way that drove in two runs in the first inning, his first two big-league RBI. He lined another single to right field in the third, and he walked in the eighth.</p><p>“Today was good,” Gonzalez said. “Obviously, I walked yesterday left on left and walked today. Those feel better than hits sometimes. It means you’re seeing it well.”</p><p>Though manager Will Venable handed first base to Gonzalez with Munetaka Murakami recovering from a strained hamstring, no one is expecting him to replace Murakami’s production. But he certainly can provide some pop, as evidenced by his 19 home runs in 52 games this season at Triple-A Charlotte.</p><p>“It’s really nice to see,” Venable said, “especially a young player in this league, you’re getting your footing and to be able to get results is great, especially after a run there where there were some strikeouts.”</p><p>Gonzalez isn’t just learning how to hit in the big leagues. He’s also learning how to play first base. Of his 52 games at Charlotte, he started 35 at shortstop and only five at first — and those were his first games there since the Sox drafted him 15th overall out of Mississippi in 2023.</p><p>It showed in the third inning Tuesday, when the Twins’ Alex Jackson bunted a ball that was fielded by pitcher Davis Martin. The problem was that Gonzalez had moved for the ball, too, and when Martin threw to him, Gonzalez didn’t get back to the base in time to touch it. He didn’t realize he had veered too far.</p><p>“I was just thinking, I know I should’ve gone to the base first and turned around,” Gonzalez said. “But [Davis] was looking at me already, [so] I’ll just catch it and touch the base as I’m catching it. And I just wasn’t where I was supposed to be.</p><p>“So I will try to never do that again. I’ll just go to the base, step on it and turn around. I’ve never had to worry about going to cover a base on a ground ball.”</p><p>Despite the mistake, which led to a run, Venable stuck by Gonzalez after the game.</p><p>“He’s here to play first base for us,” Venable said. “We’re gonna continue to support him, and he's still gonna be working hard every day to go out there and do his job.”</p><p>He did that Wednesday with a big day at the plate, which included catching up to a 98.7 mph fastball away and sending it to the opposite field at 105.5 mph.</p><p>“It’s nice to have that club in the bag,” Venable said of lining a pitch the other way. “Obviously, he’s been slugging a ton in Charlotte. Still feel like he’s gonna do damage up there. But to use the whole field, that’s how you’re gonna survive here.</p><p>“You’ve gotta be able to move the ball forward and on some tough pitches on the outside of the plate. He did a great job of that.”</p><h3>ON DECK</h3><p><b>SOX AT PHILLIES</b></p><p><b>Friday:</b> Anthony Kay (5-1, 3.77 ERA) vs. TBA, 5:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p><b>Saturday:</b> Sean Burke (2-3, entries.summary: <h3>Good morning, Chicago. ✶</h3><p>🔎 <b>Below</b>: Chicago Police Officer David Ross was on medical leave, purportedly recovering from a knee injury sustained during an on-duty crash, when he took the exam to join the mounted patrol — successfully climbing onto a horse and lifting five bales of hay, records show.</p><p>🗞️ <b>Plus</b>: The family of Spencer Leak Jr. is comforted by the many families he once helped, nurses allege retaliation over unionization efforts and more news you need to know.</p><p>📝 <b>Keeping score</b>: <a class="Link" faces firing after passing rigorous test for horseback unit while on injury leave</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whdddg-l-d/" target="_blank" >Sophie Sherry</a></h5><p><b>Mounting problems</b>: David Ross passed the strenuous test to join the Chicago Police Department’s mounted patrol in 2023 by climbing onto a horse, lifting five bales of hay and moving a 1,200-pound dumpster, among other things. Ross was on medical leave at the time and supposedly recovering from an "unbearable" knee injury sustained during an on-duty crash, records show.</p><p><b>Calls for firing</b>: Police investigators recommended that Ross be fired for violating the department’s leave policy, according to the city’s Civilian Office of Police Accountability. Records show police lawyers are still reviewing the case, and Supt. Larry Snelling hasn’t filed formal charges seeking Ross’ dismissal. It’s one of at least four disciplinary cases involving Ross that haven’t been finalized.</p><p><b>Other alleged misconduct</b>: A newly released COPA report shows Ross was given a six-month suspension for <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whdddg-l-h/" target="_blank" >choking a boy</a> who was having a mental health episode in 2024. Ross has been named in more than a dozen complaints throughout his nearly 12-year police career, records show. He has been relieved of his police powers for nearly two years and reassigned to the One of their bestselling cookies is buko pandan.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whdddg-l-ju/" target="_blank" >Pandan trend hits Chicago’s bakeries, bars and restaurants</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whdddg-l-tl/" target="_blank" >Erica Thompson</a></h5><p>A tropical plant from Southeast Asia has taken root on menus at bakeries and restaurants across Chicago.</p><p>Known for its floral taste and bright green color, pandan — specifically the leaves — is becoming a go-to ingredient for several local chefs, from Pilsen to Albany Park. Right now, they are using it to enhance cakes, cookies, ice cream, lattes and cocktails.</p><p>Of course, pandan has long been used in Southeast Asia, often in place of vanilla. Some cooks macerate its long leaves to produce green powders, extracts or juices. Others use it to create infusions to flavor everything from syrups to sticky rice. </p><p>Growing up in the Philippines, Katrina Requiron remembers eating buko pandan, a fruit salad-like dessert with young coconut and cream. At Crumbs.nd.Creams, she and her husband, co-owner Mharloe Requiron, have captured that taste in their buko pandan sylvanas, Filipino sandwich cookies. Buko pandan buttercream is tucked between two pandan-flavored cashew meringue wafers, which are dusted in cake and cookie crumbs.</p><p>Katrina began making the cookies years ago as a treat for her family. But she started to get requests from friends when Mharloe posted photos on Facebook. The demand grew, and the Algonquin couple decided to open their bakery in September. They have a significant number of Filipino customers.</p><p>"They’re like, 'Oh my God, nobody makes that here,'" Mharloe said. "I love hearing stories like that, when someone would come here and say, 'The last time I had this was back in the Philippines.'" </p><p>But they also enjoy introducing others to the treat.</p><p>"The community has been very supportive," Katrina said. "We’re just so lucky and glad that they accepted us."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whdddg-l-tr/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What is your favorite patio or rooftop in Chicago? entries.title: Passengers fight, one stabbed aboard CTA Blue Line in Loop
entries.summary: <p>A CTA Blue Line passenger pulled out a sharp object and plunged it into another passenger's neck Wednesday night in the Loop. </p><p>It unfolded around 7:25 p.m. in the 500 block of South LaSalle Street when a 36-year-old man began fighting with an another passenger he didn't know, Chicago police said. </p><p>The passenger, brandishing a sharp object, and stabbed the 36-year-old man before fleeing, police said. </p><p>He was taken to Stroger Hospital with cuts to his neck and body and was listed in fair condition, authorities said. </p><p>Area 3 detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: 2 men critically wounded in shootout at Auburn Gresham home
entries.summary: <p>A fight between two men erupted into a shootout that left both critically hurt early Thursday in the Auburn Gresham neighborhood.</p><p>The men, 39 and 33, began fighting at the home in the 1500 block of West 77th Street when they both opened fire, Chicago police said. </p><p>The older man was shot in the buttocks and the 33-year-old suffered multiple shots to his body, police said. </p><p>Both were taken to the Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn where they were listed in critical conditions, officials said. </p><p>Two guns were recovered at the scene. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: SUV hits boy, 4, in Woodlawn
entries.summary: <p>A traffic accident left a 4-year-old boy recovering at a hospital in fair condition Wednesday night in Woodlawn on the South Side.</p><p>The boy was between parked vehicles when he darted into the street where a white SUV driven by a 47-year-old woman hit him in the 6600 block of South Evans Avenue around 8:30 p.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Comer Children's Hospital where he was in fair condition, police said. </p><p>No citations were issued. </p>
